sections.html:
Heros have been exported from Venezuela since at least 1992. These fish were thought, according to scientific and hobby publications, to belong to Heros severus Heckel, 1840.

All the Heros liberifer currently available show the species-specific pattern perfectly, so wild-collected specimens of this very beautiful mouthbrooding species can be found.

Heros liberifer comes from the Rio Orinoco drainage in Venezuela. Two different species of Heros live syntopically there: this species and another one, H. severus (named in the hobby so far most often H. sp. "Inirida").

In 1994 the aquarium community learned, to its fascination, that these "real" H. severus (all other Heros in the hobby belong to different species of Heros) are larvophilous mouthbrooders, meaning the parents carry the newly hatched young in the mouth rather than the eggs.

The specific name liberifer means "carrier of children" and refers to this larvophilous mouthbrooding behaviour, which is unique in the genus.

Recent collections by travelling aquarists in Venezuela showed that two different species of Heros live syntopically there: the "mouthbrooder" and another species (Peter Dittrich, DCG-Info 2014: 21-24). This inspired Wolfgang Staeck and Ingo Schindler to re-examine the holotype of Heros severus. They found that the mouthbrooder is an undescribed species, which they named Heros liberifer.

H. liberifer can be distinguished from all other described species of Heros by its pattern: parallel rows of red spots on the lower part of the body; a clearly visible caudal spot in adults (in all other Heros species the caudal spot merges with the vertical dark bar on the caudal peduncle in adults); and small dark spots on the cheek and operculum in males (versus large dark spots or a worm-like pattern).

H. liberifer is distinguished from the at least sometimes syntopic H. severus by the following features: the iris of the eye is bright red (versus brown or dark red in H. severus); several anatomical details that cannot be recognised in living animals; and the vertical dark bar number four (counted from the tail to the head), which is shortened in H. severus and runs only to the lateral line, while in H. liberifer it runs from the base of the anal fin to the base of the dorsal fin.

Sadly, this very easy-to-see feature, the shortened vertical dark bar 4, is reliable only in wild-collected specimens. In bred fish, unwanted hybridisations have sometimes appeared, because these fish sometimes show great variation in this feature.

In all specimens studied for the description of H. liberifer, the feature of vertical bar 4 appeared quite reliable, although Schindler (DCG-Info 2015: 117) had already stated that exceptions rarely occur. Among the animals photographed for identification immediately after arrival in June, one specimen had the bar-four pattern of H. severus but the coloration of H. liberifer. It could not be established whether the shortened bar 4 appeared on both sides of the body, and the animal had already been sold. The species-specific coloration (eye, red dots etc.) of that specimen fitted H. liberifer perfectly.

Staeck, W. & I. Schindler (2015): Description of a new Heros species (Teleostei, Cichlidae) from the Rio Orinoco drainage and notes on Heros severus Heckel, 1840. Bulletin of Fish Biology 15 (1/2): 121-136
